questions.question: What causes a NullPointerException in Java and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: NullPointerException — Causes and Prevention
questions.direct_answer: A NullPointerException occurs when Java needs an object or array but the reference is null—for example, invoking a method, reading a field or array length, indexing a null array, synchronizing on null, or unboxing a null wrapper. Prevent it by defining null contracts, validating required inputs, initializing state, and representing optional results clearly; `Optional` is mainly useful as a return type, not a universal replacement for null.

sections.title: Understanding NullPointerException
sections.content:
A **NullPointerException** means an operation required an object or array reference but received `null`. Common examples are `name.length()`, `order.id`, `items.length`, `items[0]`, `synchronized(lock)`, and auto-unboxing a null `Integer` to `int`.

The useful question is not only where the dereference occurred, but why a value that was required became absent. A constructor may accept an invalid dependency, a map lookup may legitimately return null, a repository contract may be unclear, or an object may be published before initialization.

Use `Objects.requireNonNull` at required boundaries, create valid objects through constructors, and give absence a deliberate API. `Optional<T>` can communicate an optional return value, but it is not intended as a blanket field, parameter, or serialization strategy.

sections.title: NullPointerException at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Common causes|~dereferencing null|Calling a method on a null reference|Accessing a field of null|Auto-unboxing a null Integer|Map.get() that returned null
emerald|Prevention|~guard against null|Objects.requireNonNull at boundaries|Optional instead of null returns|Null checks before use|Initialize collections to empty
blue|Java help|~find it fast|Helpful NullPointerExceptions (JDK 14+)|Message names the exact null variable

sections.title: Preventing NullPointerException with Optional and Validation
When to Apply NPE Prevention Strategies
sections.content:
Use **Optional<T>** for return types when a method might legitimately have no result, like database lookups or search operations. This makes nullability part of the method contract.

Use **null checks at service boundaries** when accepting external input from REST controllers or message queues — validate parameters before processing.

Use **Objects.requireNonNull()** in constructors to fail fast when required dependencies are missing during object creation. In Spring Boot applications, constructor injection with required dependencies prevents null fields in services and repositories.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking for null after every call**: Freshers scatter if (value != null) checks everywhere instead of designing methods to return non-null values or Optional. This makes code unreadable and misses the root cause.
- **Returning null from methods**: Returning null forces every caller to remember to check, creating NPE landmines throughout the codebase. Return Optional or an empty collection instead.
- **Not validating constructor parameters**: Allowing null to be stored in fields during object creation means the NPE happens far from the source, making debugging harder.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- NPE occurs when an operation requires an object/array but the reference is null
- Method calls, field access, array use, synchronization, and unboxing can trigger it
- Read the message and frame, then trace where null entered the path
- Validate required dependencies and define absence explicitly
- `Optional` is useful for selected return contracts, not every nullable value

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: NullPointerException happens when you try to use a reference variable that's pointing to null instead of an actual object. It's the most common runtime exception you'll see in Java. The JVM throws it when you call a method or access a field on null. For example, if you do String name equals null and then call name dot length, you get an NPE because there's no String object to call length on. The modern way to prevent this is using Optional. When a method might not have a result, like looking up a user by ID, you return Optional of User instead of just User. That way the caller sees in the method signature that the value might be absent, and they're forced to handle it with methods like orElse or ifPresent. You also prevent NPEs by validating inputs at boundaries. In a REST controller, check if the incoming ID parameter is null before passing it to your service layer. In constructors, use Objects dot requireNonNull to fail immediately if someone tries to inject a null dependency. One mistake freshers make is thinking you should just add null checks everywhere. That's a code smell. If you're checking for null constantly, it means you're allowing nulls too deep into your code. Design your methods to return Optional or non-null values, and validate at entry points. That way the rest of your code can assume values exist and be much cleaner. In Spring Boot apps, constructor injection helps a lot because Spring won't create the bean if it can't satisfy the dependencies, so your service fields are never null.

questions.question: What causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java?
questions.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java
questions.direct_answer: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException occurs when you try to access an array with an index that's negative or greater than or equal to the array's length. Java arrays are zero-indexed, so valid indices run from 0 to length minus 1.

sections.title: Understanding ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
sections.content:
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` means an array access used an index outside its valid range. An array with length 5 accepts indices 0 through 4; `values[5]` and `values[-1]` both fail.

The usual causes are an off-by-one loop condition, an index calculated from untrusted input, or using the length of one collection to index another. Check the index value and the array length at the failing line. A normal forward loop uses `i < values.length`, not `i <= values.length`.

sections.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
sections.content:
rose|Cause|~bad index|Index < 0 or >= length|Off-by-one in loops (<= length)|Empty array accessed at [0]
emerald|Prevention|~bound checks|Loop with i < arr.length|Validate index before access|Use enhanced for-each when possible
blue|Note|~runtime only|Unchecked RuntimeException|Not caught at compile time

sections.title: Common ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException Scenarios
When to Guard Against This Exception
sections.content:
Use **explicit bounds checks** when the index comes from external input, like REST API parameters or file parsing, before using it to access an array.

Use **enhanced for-loops** (for-each) instead of index-based loops when you need to process every element, eliminating index arithmetic entirely.

Use **ArrayList instead of arrays** in most application code — ArrayList's get() method throws IndexOutOfBoundsException with better error messages, and methods like size() prevent confusion with array.length. In Spring Boot REST controllers, validate array indices from path variables or request parameters before passing them to array lookups.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using <= in loop conditions**: Writing for (int i = 0; i <= array.length; i++) is the classic mistake. The last valid index is length minus 1, so this always crashes on the final iteration.
- **Confusing length with size**: Arrays use .length (a field), but ArrayList uses .size() (a method). Mixing these up causes compilation errors or logic bugs.
- **Not validating calculated indices**: When you compute an index from user input or business logic, freshers forget to check if it's within bounds before accessing the array, causing crashes in production.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Zero-indexed arrays**: valid indices range from 0 to length minus 1, not 1 to length
**Off-by-one errors**: using <= instead of < in loop conditions causes access beyond the array end
**array.length**: a public final field (not a method) that returns the total number of elements
**Enhanced for-loop**: for (Type item : array) eliminates index management and prevents this exception
**ArrayList.get()**: provides clearer error messages than array indexing and is preferred in application code

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException happens when you try to access an array element using an invalid index. Arrays in Java are zero-indexed, which means if you have an array of length 5, the valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Trying to access index 5 or any negative index throws this exception. The most common cause is off-by-one errors in loops. Freshers often write for (int i equals 0; i less-than-or-equals array dot length; i plus plus), which seems logical but fails. When i reaches the array length, that's one past the last valid index, so the exception is thrown. The correct condition is i less-than array dot length. Another common scenario is when you calculate an index from user input. Say a user selects item number 3 from a menu. If you directly use that number as an array index without checking if it's within bounds, you risk crashing. You should validate that the index is at least 0 and less than the array length before accessing. The modern approach is to avoid raw arrays when possible. In most application code, use ArrayList instead. It has a get method that throws IndexOutOfBoundsException with a clearer message telling you what went wrong. Even better, use enhanced for-loops when you need to process every element. That eliminates index management completely, so you can't make the mistake. In REST APIs, if you're accepting an array index as a path variable, always validate it before using it to look up data. Return a 400 Bad Request if it's out of bounds rather than letting the exception crash your application.

questions.question: What is a ClassCastException in Java and when does it occur?
questions.title: ClassCastException in Java
questions.direct_answer: ClassCastException occurs at runtime when you try to cast an object to a type it's not actually an instance of. For example, casting a String stored in an Object reference to Integer fails because String is not an Integer subclass.

sections.title: Understanding ClassCastException
sections.content:
ClassCastException happens when you tell Java "this object is a specific type" but at runtime it turns out you're wrong.

Think of it like claiming a box labeled "Electronics" definitely contains a laptop, but when you open it, there's a toaster inside. Java checks the actual object type at runtime before allowing the cast. **WHY runtime not compile-time**: The compiler can't always know the actual object type — it only sees the declared reference type. If a method returns Object, the compiler doesn't know if that Object is really a String, Integer, or something else. **HOW it occurs**: Most commonly when working with raw collections (pre-Java 5) or downcasting in inheritance hierarchies without checking the actual type first. Modern Java uses **generics** to push these checks to compile time, making ClassCastException much rarer in well-written code. When you use List<String> instead of raw List, the compiler guarantees type safety.

sections.title: ClassCastException
sections.content:
rose|Cause|~invalid downcast|Casting to an incompatible type|Raw generics hiding the real type|Wrong type pulled from a collection
emerald|Prevention|~check first|instanceof before casting|Pattern matching: if (o instanceof Dog d)|Use generics to keep types safe
blue|Note|~runtime RuntimeException|Compiler allows the cast|JVM detects mismatch at runtime

sections.title: ClassCastException Scenarios and Prevention
When ClassCastException Becomes a Concern
sections.content:
You'll encounter ClassCastException when **deserializing JSON or XML** without proper type information, where libraries might return generic Object types that need casting. It happens in **polymorphic code** where you store different subtypes in a parent-type collection and later need to downcast to specific types. You see it when **integrating with legacy code** that uses raw collections without generics.

Use **instanceof checks** before casting when you're unsure of the actual runtime type.

Use **generics** (List<T>, Map<K,V>) in all new code to catch type errors at compile time. In Spring Boot, ClassCastException can occur when deserializing request bodies if the JSON structure doesn't match your DTO class.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming reference type equals actual type**: Freshers see Object obj = "Hello" and think obj is an Object, forgetting that the actual instance is a String. The reference type is just what the variable can hold, not what's actually there.
- **Casting without instanceof check**: Directly casting without verifying the type first leads to runtime crashes. Always check instanceof before downcasting in production code.
- **Using raw collections**: Not using generics and relying on manual casting everywhere is error-prone and was necessary before Java 5 but is now considered bad practice.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **ClassCastException**: runtime exception when casting an object to a type it's not an instance of
**instanceof operator**: checks if an object is an instance of a specific class before casting, preventing exceptions
**Pattern matching**: Java 16+ combines instanceof and casting in one step with instanceof Type variable syntax
**Generics**: introduced in Java 5 to enforce type safety at compile time and eliminate most ClassCastExceptions
**Upcasting vs downcasting**: upcasting (subtype to supertype) is always safe, downcasting requires runtime checks

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: ClassCastException happens when you try to cast an object to a type it isn't actually an instance of at runtime. The key thing to understand is the difference between the reference type and the actual object type. If I write Object obj equals "Hello", the reference type is Object but the actual object in memory is a String. Now if I try to cast that to Integer, like Integer num equals (Integer) obj, the compiler allows it because obj is declared as Object, which could theoretically hold an Integer. But at runtime, the JVM checks the actual type and sees it's a String, not an Integer, so it throws ClassCastException. The way to prevent this is using the instanceof operator before casting. You write if (obj instanceof String) and only cast inside that block. Modern Java makes this even nicer with pattern matching. You can write if (obj instanceof String str) and the variable str is automatically created as a String, so no manual cast needed. The biggest improvement came with generics in Java 5. When you use List of String instead of a raw List, the compiler enforces that only Strings go into that list. When you call get, you get a String directly with no casting required. All the type checking happens at compile time, so you can't get a ClassCastException from that collection. Freshers often get confused because they think the compiler checks everything about types. It doesn't. The compiler only checks what it can see from the declared types. At runtime, the actual object might be something different, which is when ClassCastException happens. That's why modern Java emphasizes generics — they let the compiler verify more at compile time so you avoid runtime surprises.

questions.question: When does NumberFormatException occur in Java and how do you handle it?
questions.title: NumberFormatException in Java
questions.direct_answer: `NumberFormatException` occurs when a string cannot be parsed in the format required by a numeric method such as `Integer.parseInt`. Examples include an empty string, `"12.5"` passed to `parseInt`, or a value outside the `int` range. At an input boundary, trim only if the contract permits it, call the correct parser, catch `NumberFormatException`, and return a clear validation error or another result that represents invalid input.

sections.title: Understanding NumberFormatException
sections.content:
`NumberFormatException` is thrown when a numeric parser cannot convert its text to the requested Java number. `Integer.parseInt("42")` works, but `Integer.parseInt("")`, `Integer.parseInt("12.5")`, and an integer larger than the `int` range fail. Different parsers accept different formats; for example, `Double.parseDouble` accepts decimal and scientific notation, including special floating-point values such as `NaN`.

Parse at the boundary where text enters the program. Decide whether surrounding spaces, signs, decimal points, or separators are allowed by that input contract. Then use the matching parser and handle `NumberFormatException` close enough to return a useful message. A regular expression is not a full replacement for the parser because range and format rules still matter.

sections.title: NumberFormatException
sections.content:
rose|Cause|~unparseable text|Integer.parseInt("abc")|Empty or null string|Whitespace / commas / symbols
emerald|Prevention|~validate & trim|trim() and check not empty|Regex/matches before parsing|try-catch around parse for user input
blue|Note|~subclass of IllegalArgumentException|Unchecked exception|Thrown by parseInt / parseDouble / valueOf

sections.title: Handling NumberFormatException in REST API
When to Apply NumberFormatException Handling
sections.content:
Use **try-catch** for NumberFormatException when parsing user input in REST controllers, accepting form data, or processing uploaded files like CSV. The exception tells you the input was invalid, and you should return a 400 Bad Request status code.

Use **pre-validation with regex** when you want to validate format before parsing, like checking if a string contains only digits using matches("\\d+") before calling parseInt.

Use **Optional return types** in utility methods that parse strings, returning Optional.empty() on parse failure instead of throwing exceptions, which gives callers more flexibility. In Spring Boot validation, use the at-Pattern annotation on DTO fields to validate numeric string formats before they reach your parsing logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Letting exceptions propagate**: Freshers allow NumberFormatException to bubble up to the framework, resulting in generic 500 errors shown to users. Always catch it at the controller layer and return a proper 400 with a meaningful message.
- **Not trimming whitespace**: Calling parseInt on " 123 " (with spaces) throws NumberFormatException. Always trim input strings before parsing.
- **Parsing without validation**: Calling parseInt on every user input without checking format first makes your API fragile. Validate or wrap in try-catch to handle bad input gracefully.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **NumberFormatException**: unchecked exception thrown by parseInt, parseDouble when the string isn't a valid number
**Common causes**: empty strings, strings with letters, leading/trailing whitespace, incorrect decimal separators
**HTTP status codes**: catch NumberFormatException in REST controllers and return 400 Bad Request, not 500 Internal Server Error
**String.matches()**: validate numeric format with regex patterns before parsing to avoid exceptions entirely
**String.trim()**: always trim user input before parsing to remove leading/trailing whitespace that causes failures

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `NumberFormatException` means a numeric parsing method received text that is not valid for its target type. For example, `Integer.parseInt("12.5")` fails because an integer parser does not accept a decimal point, and a very large sequence of digits can fail because it is outside the `int` range. I handle it where the text enters the system: apply the documented trimming rule, call the correct parser, catch this specific exception, and return a clear validation result. I do not depend only on a regular expression, because the parser also enforces range and exact format rules.

questions.question: What is the difference between a checked exception and an unchecked exception in Java?
questions.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
questions.direct_answer: A checked exception is a subclass of `Exception` that is not a subclass of `RuntimeException`; Java requires a caller to catch it or declare it with `throws`. An unchecked exception is a `RuntimeException` subclass and has no catch-or-declare requirement. `Error` is also unchecked but represents a separate throwable branch. Checked versus unchecked does not by itself decide whether a condition is recoverable.

sections.title: Understanding Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
sections.content:
Java's **catch-or-declare** rule applies to checked exceptions: subclasses of `Exception` other than `RuntimeException`. A method that can let one escape must declare it, and its caller must catch it or declare it further.

`RuntimeException` and its subclasses are unchecked. The compiler allows them to propagate without a `throws` clause. `Error` is also unchecked, but it is not an exception subtype and commonly represents JVM or environment failures that normal application code should not broadly catch.

The categories are language rules, not a perfect map of recoverability. A checked `IOException` may not be recoverable at the current layer, while an unchecked validation exception may be translated into a clear 400 response. Choose an API based on who can act on the failure and preserve causes when translating it.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
sections.content:
blue|Checked|~compiler-enforced|Extends Exception (not RuntimeException)|Must declare with throws or catch|IOException, SQLException|Recoverable, expected conditions
rose|Unchecked|~runtime|Extends RuntimeException|No compile-time requirement|NullPointer, IllegalArgument|Usually programming bugs
emerald|Root|~hierarchy|Throwable -> Exception / Error|Error (OutOfMemory) = don't catch

rows: Caller can meaningfully recover or retry
Indicates bug that should be fixed in code

sections.title: Checked exception — compiler forces handling
Unchecked exception — no compiler ceremony
When to Use Each Type
sections.content:
Use **checked exceptions** when the failure is outside your control and the caller might want to recover. Examples: file operations where the file might not exist, database queries that might time out, parsing JSON that might be malformed. The caller should decide whether to retry, use a default value, or notify the user.

Use **unchecked exceptions** for programming errors like null arguments passed to a method that requires non-null, negative values where only positive makes sense, or accessing a collection beyond its size. These indicate bugs that should be fixed during development, not runtime conditions to handle. In REST APIs, throw unchecked exceptions for validation failures and use exception handlers to convert them to appropriate HTTP status codes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Catching Exception directly**: Writing catch (Exception e) catches everything including unchecked exceptions you shouldn't handle generically. Catch specific checked exceptions you expect.
- **Declaring throws Exception**: Method signatures with throws Exception are too broad. Declare the specific checked exceptions callers need to know about.
- **Making custom exceptions checked by default**: Freshers extend Exception for custom errors without thinking. Usually business logic exceptions should be unchecked (extend RuntimeException) so they don't force boilerplate throughout the code.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Checked**: `Exception` subtype excluding `RuntimeException`; catch or declare
- **Unchecked exception**: `RuntimeException` subtype; no catch-or-declare rule
- **`Error`**: also unchecked, but a separate branch from exceptions
- The compiler category does not guarantee recoverability
- Translate failures at meaningful boundaries and preserve the original cause

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A checked exception is an `Exception` subtype other than `RuntimeException`, and Java's compiler requires it to be caught or declared. `IOException` is a common example. An unchecked exception is a `RuntimeException` subtype, such as `IllegalArgumentException`, so the compiler does not impose catch-or-declare. `Error` is also unchecked but belongs to a different branch of `Throwable`. The distinction is a language rule, not a promise that checked conditions are recoverable or unchecked ones are always programmer bugs. I choose handling based on what the current layer can meaningfully do, while preserving the original cause when translating exceptions.

questions.question: What is the finally block and when is it executed?
questions.title: The finally Block
questions.direct_answer: A `finally` block normally runs when control leaves its matching `try`, whether by normal completion, `return`, or an exception. It is not an absolute guarantee: JVM termination, process failure, forced halt, or code that never leaves the `try` can prevent it. Prefer try-with-resources for `AutoCloseable` resources because it closes them in reverse order and preserves close failures as suppressed exceptions.

sections.title: Understanding the Finally Block
sections.content:
A `finally` block runs as control exits its `try` statement after the selected `catch` path, including when the code returns or throws. That makes it suitable for restoring state or releasing a resource that cannot use a higher-level construct.

It is not guaranteed under every possible event. `System.exit`, `Runtime.halt`, a killed process, JVM crash, power loss, or a `try` that never completes can prevent execution. A `return` or new exception inside `finally` is also dangerous because it can replace the original return value or failure.

For files, sockets, and JDBC objects that implement `AutoCloseable`, use try-with-resources. Java closes resources in reverse declaration order and retains close failures as suppressed exceptions when another exception is already primary.

sections.title: try-catch-finally Execution Order
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A[Enter try] --> B{Exception thrown?}
  B -->|no| C[try completes]
  B -->|yes| D[Matching catch runs]
  C --> E[finally normally runs]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Method returns / propagates]
  E -.->|even on return or throw| F
```
*`finally` normally runs when control leaves `try` or `catch`, including by `return` or `throw`. It is not guaranteed if the JVM or process stops abruptly; try-with-resources is preferred for closeable resources.

sections.title: Finally Block vs Try-With-Resources
When to Use Finally vs Try-With-Resources
sections.content:
Use **try-with-resources** for any resource that implements AutoCloseable, including files, database connections, streams, and HTTP clients. It's cleaner and handles multiple resources better, automatically closing them in reverse order of creation.

Use **finally** only when you need cleanup logic that isn't resource closing, like resetting a flag, logging completion, or releasing a lock. In Spring Boot, prefer try-with-resources for JDBC ResultSet and Statement objects to ensure proper connection pool cleanup.

Avoid finally when try-with-resources can do the job — it eliminates boilerplate and prevents mistakes like forgetting null checks or double-closing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting null check in finally**: Calling resource.close() without checking if resource is null first causes NullPointerException if the resource wasn't successfully created.
- **Not knowing finally runs on return**: Freshers think return statements exit immediately, not realizing finally still executes afterward. This matters when finally modifies return values or closes resources.
- **Using finally for resources with AutoCloseable**: Writing manual finally blocks for file or database cleanup when try-with-resources is simpler and less error-prone. Try-with-resources should be the default choice now.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `finally` normally runs when control leaves `try`/`catch`, including return and throw
- Process or JVM termination and non-terminating code can prevent it
- Do not return from `finally` or hide the primary exception
- Prefer try-with-resources for `AutoCloseable` resources
- Try-with-resources closes in reverse order and can retain suppressed failures

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A `finally` block normally executes when control leaves the associated `try`, whether the code completes normally, returns, or throws and unwinds. I use it for cleanup or state restoration that must follow that control flow. It is not an absolute guarantee: `System.exit`, a forced JVM halt, a killed process, or code that never leaves the `try` can prevent it. I also avoid `return` or throwing a new unrelated exception from `finally`, because that can hide the original result or failure. For an `AutoCloseable` resource such as a stream or JDBC connection, try-with-resources is safer and clearer. It closes resources in reverse declaration order and records a close failure as suppressed when another exception is already primary.
